text: Syslog is the standard logging protocol spoken by Linux servers, firewalls, routers, switches, and nearly every network device that isn't Windows-native. It usually reaches the SIEM over UDP port 514, TCP port 514 for delivery guarantees, or TCP port 6514 when it's wrapped in TLS. It's what lets a SIEM listen for logs from any vendor's hardware using one shared protocol instead of a custom listener for each device.

A raw syslog line carries more structure than it looks. Take this firewall message: PRI 34, a timestamp, the hostname, and the process that logged it, followed by the message text. That leading number isn't arbitrary — it's facility times 8 plus severity. Here, facility 4, the auth facility, times 8 is 32, plus severity 2, Critical, equals 34. A SIEM reads that value first, before parsing a single word of the message itself, which is how it instantly knows this is a security-relevant event at a serious severity.

Syslog defines exactly eight severity levels, numbered 0 through 7: Emergency, Alert, Critical, Error, Warning, Notice, Informational, and Debug. These levels let a correlation rule filter by threshold — watching only for Error or worse, for instance, while ignoring routine Informational chatter — and let a SOC exclude noisy Debug-level devices from ingestion entirely so they don't flood the platform with volume nobody will ever review.

Raw syslog only standardizes the envelope; the message body can still be anything a vendor wants. CEF, the Common Event Format from ArcSight, and LEEF, IBM QRadar's equivalent, fix that by writing the event body as standardized key-value pairs: src=, dst=, spt=, dpt=. One parser then reads Cisco, Palo Alto, or Check Point the same way, instead of a handwritten parser per vendor, which is exactly what makes onboarding a new log source fast instead of a weeks-long parsing project.

Syslog gets the message to the SIEM reliably, across almost any vendor's hardware. CEF and LEEF make what's inside that message predictable enough to parse at scale, the same way, every time. Next: Windows doesn't speak syslog natively, so Lesson 10 covers Windows Event Forwarding — the subscription-based way Windows logs reach a central collector instead, without a third-party agent.
